title: Safe Assessment: What It Means and How Security Teams Run One
summary: "Safe assessment" can mean SAFe agile reviews, CISA's SAFE or a vendor security review. Here is how to tell them apart and answer security assessments faster.
body_markdown:
A search for "safe assessment" returns at least four different things: the SAFe agile assessments from Scaled Agile, CISA's Security Assessment at First Entry (SAFE), a child-welfare home study method, and a clinical swallowing evaluation. If you work in security, risk, compliance or enterprise sales, the assessment you meet most often is a different one: the security assessment a customer sends before it signs a contract. This guide sorts out the meanings in a few lines, then covers what matters to your team: how to prepare, run and repeat a security assessment without losing deals or weeks of engineering time. ## TL;DR


- "Safe assessment" is ambiguous. SAFe (capital E) is an agile framework, CISA's SAFE is a physical security review, and the other results are social-care and clinical tools.
- For B2B software, security, GRC and sales teams, the assessment that blocks revenue is the customer's security questionnaire or due diligence review.
- Good assessments share a pattern: define scope, gather evidence, analyze results, act, and repeat on a schedule.
- The slow part is rarely the thinking. It is finding past answers, routing questions to experts and re-typing into customer portals.
- Automating that work with a governed answer library and confidence scoring is how teams shorten turnaround without lowering accuracy.

## The meanings of "safe assessment" in one minute


Before going further, here is how the main results break down, so you can confirm you are in the right place.


Term What it is Who uses it


SAFe Business Agility and Measure and Grow assessments Surveys that gauge progress toward business agility Agile coaches, portfolio and program leaders


Security Assessment at First Entry (SAFE) A rapid physical security review of a facility Facility owners and operators, with CISA staff


Security assessment (vendor review) Questionnaires and evidence requests a buyer uses to judge a supplier's controls CISOs, GRC and sales engineering teams


SAFE home study, swallowing evaluation Social-care and clinical protocols Child welfare agencies, health professionals


The last row is for a different reader, so we leave it there. The first two get a short explanation below because teams in software companies often run into both. The third is the focus of the rest of this article.


## SAFe assessments: agile maturity, not security


The Scaled Agile Framework describes[Measure and Grow](https://framework.scaledagile.com/measure-and-grow) as the approach enterprises use to evaluate progress toward business agility and decide on improvement actions. It looks at outcomes, flow and competency: whether solutions meet customer and business needs, how efficiently value is delivered, and how proficient the organization is in the practices that enable agility.


If your engineering organization runs SAFe, you may be asked to take part. The pattern is useful beyond agile work. Scaled Agile's[facilitation guidance](https://framework.scaledagile.com/facilitating-safe-assessments) describes a standard sequence for each assessment: run it, analyze the results, take action and celebrate the wins. Its team assessment guide also says to[define a shared purpose first](https://scaledagile.com/blog/measuring-team-and-technical-agility-guide/) , and recommends a trained facilitator because teams can feel defensive about being measured and self-reported data is not always objective.


Those lessons carry over directly to security reviews, as the next sections show.


## CISA's SAFE: a physical security review


The other acronym match is the[Security Assessment at First Entry](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/services/security-assessment-first-entry) from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). It is a rapid physical security assessment in which CISA Protective Security Advisors give a structured review of a facility's existing security measures and feedback on observed vulnerabilities and options for improvement. You request it through your local CISA field staff or regional office. If you operate data centers or offices that a customer asks about, the findings can feed your answers on physical security, but it is a facility review, not a questionnaire process.


## The assessment that decides deals: the customer security review


For a B2B software company, the assessment that most directly affects revenue is the one your customer's risk team sends. It usually arrives as a spreadsheet, a portal login, or a standard questionnaire such as SIG or a due diligence questionnaire (DDQ). A DDQ is a structured list of questions a buyer, often in finance, uses to evaluate a supplier or manager before committing. Its questions cover access control, encryption, incident response, business continuity, privacy and increasingly AI governance.


Three groups feel it at once:


- **Sales and solution engineers** wait on answers while a deal stalls. Security review is often the last gate before signature.
- **CISOs and GRC leads** are pulled from planned work to confirm answers they have already given many times.
- **Customers' risk teams** want consistent, evidence-backed responses they can compare across vendors.


Skypher's own[SIG assessment guide](https://skypher.co/post/sig-assessment-guide-2025-process-benefits-tips-en#what-is-sig-assessment-and-why-it-matters) explains how the SIG framework works and why vendors should treat it as a strategic exercise rather than paperwork.


## A five-step process for running a security assessment


The SAFe facilitation pattern and the security review pattern have the same bones. Here is how we suggest teams apply it when a questionnaire lands.


### 1. Define scope and purpose


Before anyone answers a question, settle what is being assessed: which product, which environment, which entity. Scaled Agile's[assessment workshop guidance](https://framework.scaledagile.com/blog/updated-ai-empowered-safe-assessment-workshop) starts with establishing purpose and scope so everyone knows what is measured and why. In a security review, scope errors are costly. Answering for the wrong environment creates an inconsistency that a customer's reviewer will notice later.


Write down the product version, hosting model, data types in scope and the compliance reports you will attach. Then reuse that statement on every review.


### 2. Gather evidence once, in one place


Most answers already exist: a SOC 2 report, a penetration test summary, policies, architecture diagrams, a previous questionnaire. The problem is that they live in Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, SharePoint and old spreadsheets. Teams that keep a single approved source of truth, with version control, avoid the situation where two reviewers give two different answers about encryption at rest.


Our platform connects to Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, OneDrive and SharePoint, and its content management includes document versioning, so the answer a reviewer finds is based on the current document, not a stale copy.


### 3. Answer with a first draft, then review


Scaled Agile's guidance has teams[complete assessments individually and then discuss](https://scaledagile.com/blog/measuring-team-and-technical-agility-guide/) , or discuss as a group and agree on answers. Anonymous answers are possible only in the first mode. The same logic applies to security reviews: a first draft prepared individually is faster, and a group review catches disagreements.


The practical split is simple. Generate the draft from approved content, then send only low-confidence or sensitive answers to a subject-matter expert. That keeps your CISO's time for the questions that need judgment, such as new regulatory language or custom contractual requirements.


Skypher's AI is built on proprietary retrieval models and gives each answer a confidence score, so reviewers can focus on the ones that need attention first. It parses every common questionnaire format and is designed to answer even 200 questions in under a minute.


### 4. Analyze the results and close gaps


A completed questionnaire is also a diagnostic. Scaled Agile describes[key strengths and key opportunities](https://scaledagile.com/blog/measuring-team-and-technical-agility-guide/) by comparing average scores and the spread between respondents. You can borrow the idea: questions that repeatedly get low-confidence answers, or answers where reviewers disagree, point to missing documentation or an unclear policy.


Keep a short log after each review:


1. Which questions had no approved answer.
2. Which answers a reviewer rewrote, and why.
3. Which customer follow-ups came back, and on what topic.


Then fix the source document, not just the single answer. Our[guide on analyzing findings](https://skypher.co/post/sig-assessment-guide-2025-process-benefits-tips-en#analyzing-and-implementing-assessment-findings) covers how to turn results into changes.


### 5. Repeat on a schedule


Scaled Agile suggests running its team assessment[once a program increment or once a year](https://scaledagile.com/blog/measuring-team-and-technical-agility-guide/) , depending on goals, to see progress. A sensible rhythm for security content is similar: review your answer library at least annually, and again after a major audit, a new certification, an architecture change or a significant incident. Customer questionnaires will keep arriving in between, and an answer library that was last touched two years ago is the main source of inaccurate responses.


## Where the process usually goes wrong


- **Copying from the last questionnaire.** Fast, but it carries forward outdated claims. Answers should come from governed documents with a clear owner.
- **Unclear ownership.** If nobody owns the answer on vulnerability management, it goes to whoever is online. Assign owners by topic.
- **Portals that force re-keying.** Many customers require answers entered into an online portal. Typing the same text across portals is where hours disappear. Skypher offers 30+ API connectors to online portals, including OneTrust and ServiceNow, so answers can be completed where the customer asks for them.
- **Treating it as a one-off.** Sales cycles repeat. A team that handles five reviews a month needs a system, not heroics.
- **Defensiveness.** Scaled Agile notes that people can feel judged by assessments. Customer reviews can feel the same way to engineers. Framing the work as evidence gathering, not interrogation, keeps experts responsive.


## What good looks like for each role


### CISO and GRC


You want consistent answers, traceability to source documents and the ability to approve high-risk responses. Look for a single governed library, confidence scoring to prioritize review, and an audit trail of what changed. Real-time collaboration with unlimited users matters here, because subject-matter experts in engineering, legal and IT need to contribute without license friction.


### Sales directors and solution engineers


You want shorter cycles and fewer surprises. Chatbot support in Slack and Microsoft Teams lets a rep ask a security question and get an answer from approved content without opening a ticket. Our Salesforce integration keeps the review tied to the deal. A customer-facing[Trust Center](https://skypher.co/trust-center) can also answer many questions before a questionnaire is even sent, by publishing your security posture and documents in one place.


### Finance-sector teams handling DDQs


Due diligence questionnaires are longer and more formal, and the audience is often an investor or institutional client. Our[DDQ automation page](https://skypher.co/automate-ddqs) describes how we handle that format.

## Self-assessments before the customer asks


Many teams complete an internal self-assessment first, scoring their own controls against a standard so they know their weak points before a buyer finds them. That is the same idea as the SAFe team self-assessment: reflect honestly, identify opportunities, pick a small number of improvements. ## FAQ


### What is a SAFe assessment?


It is part of the Scaled Agile Framework's Measure and Grow approach, which helps enterprises evaluate progress toward business agility. It measures outcomes, flow and competency, then points to improvement actions. It is an agile maturity tool, not a security or compliance review.


### What is the Security Assessment at First Entry (SAFE)?


It is a rapid physical security assessment offered by CISA. Protective Security Advisors review a facility's existing measures and provide feedback on vulnerabilities and options for improvement. Facility owners and operators request it through CISA's regional offices.


### How often should we repeat an assessment?


Scaled Agile recommends running its team assessment once per program increment or once a year, depending on goals. For security answer libraries, we suggest an annual review plus an update after any major audit, certification or architecture change, so that responses always match your current controls.


### Who should review answers to a security questionnaire?


A first draft can come from approved content, with subject-matter experts reviewing the answers flagged as low confidence or sensitive. The CISO or GRC lead approves anything that creates a contractual commitment. Skypher supports unlimited users collaborating in real time, so each expert can contribute directly.
